content: Adhesive capsulitis, commonly referred to as frozen shoulder, is a frequent condition encountered in primary care settings. It can develop either as a primary condition or secondary to other underlying issues. A thorough clinical examination is essential to distinguish adhesive capsulitis from other potential conditions. Below are the differential diagnoses and their distinguishing features: 1. Rotator Cuff Injury or Tendinopathy with or without Supraspinatus Impingement: Patients often report a history of overuse or repetitive shoulder activity. Focal tenderness is typically present, and passive range of motion is preserved. Diagnostic tests such as the Hawkins and Neer tests are often positive in cases of impingement. 2. Rotator Cuff Tear: This condition is characterized by severe lateral arm pain and significant limitations in both active and passive range of motion. The drop arm test is usually positive. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a key diagnostic tool for confirming a rotator cuff tear. 3. Acromioclavicular Arthropathy: Pain is localized to the superior aspect of the shoulder joint, often associated with a history of heavy weightlifting or repetitive overuse. Range of motion is typically preserved. Clinical diagnosis can be supported by positive results on the cross-arm test and compression test. 4. Subacromial Bursitis: Diagnosis can be aided by the administration of a local lidocaine injection and confirmed with MRI imaging. 5. Cervical Radiculopathy or Cervical Disc Degeneration: Patients may present with weakness, numbness, and impaired light touch sensation in the upper extremity. Active range of motion is often reduced with neck movements, suggesting cervical spine involvement. 6. Subdeltoid Bursitis: A history of overuse injury is common. MRI is useful in confirming the diagnosis. 7. Tendinopathy of the Biceps at the Bicipital Groove: Patients typically report anterior upper arm pain. Diagnostic tests such as the Speed and Yergason tests are positive. 8. Malignancy: Symptoms such as unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and compressive symptoms (e.g., from a Pancoast tumor) may raise suspicion for malignancy. Imaging studies are crucial to exclude frozen shoulder in these cases. 9. Polymyalgia Rheumatica: This condition is characterized by proximal muscle weakness affecting both the upper and lower extremities. An elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) can help differentiate it from adhesive capsulitis. 10. Autoimmune Diseases: Conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or rheumatoid arthritis may mimic the presentation of frozen shoulder. A detailed clinical evaluation and appropriate laboratory tests are necessary to identify these autoimmune conditions.
